# Lab 4 — Kubernetes: Deploy QuickTicket to a Cluster

## Task 1 — Write Manifests & Deploy to k3d

### 4.5 Test Kubernetes self-healing

The gateway pod was deleted with `kubectl delete pod -l app=gateway` while `kubectl get pods -w` was running. Kubernetes terminated the old pod and immediately created a replacement pod from the Deployment. The replacement pod moved from `Pending` to `ContainerCreating` and then to `Running`.

```text
kubectl get pods -w

NAME                         READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
events-6c4df7d6-qk7kv        1/1     Running   0          14m
gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     1/1     Running   0          51s
payments-58fb468db-pm8th     1/1     Running   0          14m
postgres-7c7ffc4b-r7w8w      1/1     Running   0          18m
redis-c46d5dffc-m4cfw        1/1     Running   0          18m

kubectl delete pod -l app=gateway
pod "gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f" deleted from default namespace

gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     1/1     Terminating         0   75s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-xlh92     0/1     Pending             0   0s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     1/1     Terminating         0   75s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-xlh92     0/1     Pending             0   1s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-xlh92     0/1     ContainerCreating   0   1s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     0/1     Completed           0   78s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     0/1     Completed           0   79s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-v6q2f     0/1     Completed           0   79s
gateway-6fc44f68c5-xlh92     1/1     Running             0   5s
```

<img alt="Task 1.5 - Kubernetes recreating the deleted gateway pod automatically" src="data:image/png;base64,">

### 4.6 Recovery time comparison

Kubernetes created the replacement gateway pod immediately after deletion, and the new pod reached `1/1 Running` at about 5 seconds of age. The old pod continued terminating in parallel before moving to `Completed`, but the Deployment controller had already restored the desired replica. This was much faster than the earlier Docker Compose workflow, where recovery required identifying the stopped component and starting it manually. In Kubernetes, the Deployment controller continuously compares the desired state with the current state, so it automatically creates a new pod when the running pod is deleted.

## Task 2 — Probes & Resource Limits

### 4.9 Add readiness and liveness probes

The application Deployments were updated with liveness probes, readiness probes, and resource requests/limits. After applying the manifests, the new Pods for `events`, `gateway`, and `payments` were running, ready, and using the configured probes.

For this implementation, readiness uses `/health` because it answers whether the service can receive traffic. Liveness uses `/metrics` as a lighter process-level check, because `/health` may include dependency checks. If liveness checks dependencies such as PostgreSQL, Redis, or another backend service, Kubernetes may restart a healthy process because of an external dependency failure.

```text
Name:             events-7666ffd844-kbk9q
Status:           Running
Containers:
  events:
    State:          Running
    Ready:          True
    Restart Count:  0
    Limits:
      cpu:     200m
      memory:  256Mi
    Requests:
      cpu:      50m
      memory:   64Mi
    Liveness:   http-get http://:8081/metrics delay=15s timeout=3s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
    Readiness:  http-get http://:8081/health delay=5s timeout=3s period=5s #success=1 #failure=2
Conditions:
  Ready                       True
  ContainersReady             True
```

```text
Name:             gateway-f8b44ff7-m62cf
Status:           Running
Containers:
  gateway:
    State:          Running
    Ready:          True
    Restart Count:  0
    Limits:
      cpu:     200m
      memory:  256Mi
    Requests:
      cpu:      50m
      memory:   64Mi
    Liveness:   http-get http://:8080/metrics delay=15s timeout=3s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
    Readiness:  http-get http://:8080/health delay=5s timeout=3s period=5s #success=1 #failure=2
Conditions:
  Ready                       True
  ContainersReady             True
```

```text
Name:             payments-57bf487cdd-ppqfn
Status:           Running
Containers:
  payments:
    State:          Running
    Ready:          True
    Restart Count:  0
    Limits:
      cpu:     200m
      memory:  256Mi
    Requests:
      cpu:      50m
      memory:   64Mi
    Liveness:   http-get http://:8082/metrics delay=15s timeout=3s period=10s #success=1 #failure=3
    Readiness:  http-get http://:8082/health delay=5s timeout=3s period=5s #success=1 #failure=2
Conditions:
  Ready                       True
  ContainersReady             True
```

### 4.10 Observe readiness probe failure

Redis was first deleted with `kubectl delete pod -l app=redis`; Kubernetes recreated it quickly. To keep the dependency unavailable long enough for the readiness threshold to trigger, the Redis Deployment was temporarily scaled to zero replicas and then restored. During the Redis interruption, the Events readiness probe failed because the Events `/health` endpoint depends on Redis. The `kubectl describe` output showed `Readiness probe failed` and `HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503`.

```text
Scaling redis to 0
deployment.apps/redis scaled
Watching events readiness while Redis is unavailable:
--- 0s ---
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
events-7c664d56bf-z9n4h   1/1     Running   0          5m59s
--- 9s ---
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
events-7c664d56bf-z9n4h   0/1     Running   0          6m21s
Events became NotReady after 9s
Readiness describe excerpt:
    Readiness:  http-get http://:8081/health delay=5s timeout=3s period=5s #success=1 #failure=2
  Warning  Unhealthy  2s (x3 over 7s)  kubelet  spec.containers{events}: Readiness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503
Restoring redis to 1
deployment.apps/redis scaled
deployment "redis" successfully rolled out
Final state:
NAME                    READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
redis-c46d5dffc-vwg4k   1/1     Running   0          12s
NAME                      READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
events-7c664d56bf-z9n4h   1/1     Running   0          6m36s
```

This demonstrates the expected readiness behavior: the application process can continue running, but Kubernetes marks the Pod as not ready while an important dependency is unavailable.

### 4.12 Liveness vs readiness

A readiness probe answers whether a Pod should receive traffic. When readiness fails, Kubernetes keeps the container running but removes that Pod from the Service endpoints until the probe passes again.

A liveness probe answers whether the container process should be restarted. When liveness fails repeatedly, Kubernetes kills and restarts the container.

Database or Redis connectivity should be checked with readiness, not liveness. If PostgreSQL or Redis is unavailable, restarting the application container does not fix that external dependency. The safer behavior is to keep the process running, stop sending traffic to it while it is degraded, and allow it to become ready again when the dependency recovers.

## Bonus Task — Helm Chart

### B.1 Chart scaffold

The Helm chart was created under `k8s/chart`. The `Chart.yaml` file defines the chart metadata, while `values.yaml` centralizes the configurable values used by the templates.

```yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: quickticket
description: QuickTicket SRE learning project
type: application
version: 0.1.0
appVersion: "v1"
```

### B.2 Configurable values

The local `values.yaml` file is heavily commented for study purposes. The version below shows the effective values without the explanatory comments.

```yaml
global:
  imagePullPolicy: Never
  serviceType: ClusterIP
  resources:
    requests:
      cpu: 50m
      memory: 64Mi
    limits:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
  probes:
    liveness:
      initialDelaySeconds: 15
      periodSeconds: 10
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 3
    readiness:
      initialDelaySeconds: 5
      periodSeconds: 5
      timeoutSeconds: 3
      failureThreshold: 2

postgres:
  replicas: 1
  image: postgres:17-alpine
  port: 5432
  database: quickticket
  user: quickticket
  password: quickticket

redis:
  replicas: 1
  image: redis:7-alpine
  port: 6379

events:
  replicas: 1
  image: quickticket-events:v1
  port: 8081
  db:
    host: postgres
    port: "5432"
    name: quickticket
    user: quickticket
    password: quickticket
    maxConns: "10"
  redis:
    host: redis
    port: "6379"
    timeoutMs: "1000"
  reservationTtl: "300"
  probes:
    livenessPath: /metrics
    readinessPath: /health

gateway:
  replicas: 1
  image: quickticket-gateway:v1
  port: 8080
  eventsUrl: http://events:8081
  paymentsUrl: http://payments:8082
  timeoutMs: "5000"
  probes:
    livenessPath: /metrics
    readinessPath: /health

payments:
  replicas: 1
  image: quickticket-payments:v1
  port: 8082
  failureRate: "0.0"
  latencyMs: "0"
  probes:
    livenessPath: /metrics
    readinessPath: /health
```
